einstellungen.text: Sunday afternoon. You're at your grandpa's place on the sixteenth floor, and you're losing at rummy for the third time.
He grins, lays down his cards and slides the last piece of apple pie over to you. A consolation prize.
Then you see it. The tea in his glass is trembling. Tiny rings on the surface. Nobody touched the table.
One second later, the whole building shakes. Glasses fly out of the cabinet, the shelf tips over, the floor sways like a ship.
"Under the table!" your grandpa shouts. You crawl under it and grab the table leg.
Forty seconds. That's how long it lasts. It feels like an hour.
What comes next are the longest seventy-two hours of your life. And in the very last hour, everything depends on a single sound.
Three forty in the afternoon.
It's quiet. The apartment looks like someone picked it up and shook it.
Your grandpa has a scrape on his forehead, but he's already smiling again. He always does that when he wants you to stop being scared.
You flip the light switch. Nothing. The fridge is silent, the clock on the stove is black.
The front door is jammed. You throw your shoulder against it, twice, three times. Then it pops open.
The stairwell smells like concrete and dust. You head down. Fifteenth floor. Fourteenth. Thirteenth.
On the twelfth floor, you stop breathing. Below you, there are no more stairs.
Where the steps used to be, there's only a hole full of rubble and twisted steel bars. Ten floors deep.
The only way down is gone. The elevator is stuck. And you and your grandpa are trapped on the sixteenth floor.
You call your mom. Busy. Again. Call failed.
After a big quake, millions of people try to make a call in the same minute. No network in the world can handle that.
So you send a text instead. A text is tiny. Sometimes it still slips through when no call can.
Grandpa and I are alive. Sixteenth floor. Stairs gone. You hit send. Under the message, a little circle starts spinning. And spinning. And spinning.
Eight thirty at night.
Outside, it's getting dark. And for the first time, you see your city without a single light. Only sirens, wailing in the distance.
Grandpa pulls candles out of a drawer. He has a drawer for everything. Candles, a camping stove, a hand-crank radio.
You always made fun of him for his emergency drawer. Today you don't say a word.
You turn on the faucet. A gurgle, a few drops. Then nothing.
In a high-rise, a pump pushes the water up to the top floors. No power, no pump. No pump, no water.
There's one bottle of water left in the apartment. Without water, a person only lasts about three days.
Three days. You do the math. For two people, one bottle is nothing.
Then it shakes again. Shorter, but hard enough that Grandpa reaches for your hand.
Aftershocks. After a major earthquake, they can keep coming for days, even weeks.
From the stairwell, you hear a rumble. More chunks of concrete falling into the hole.
Later, in the candlelight, you see your grandpa shaking his pill bottle. He's counting. And he doesn't tell you how many are left.
Monday. Ten fifteen in the morning.
You barely slept. It's cold in the apartment. No power means no heat, and it's November.
But during the night, you remembered something. Something your grandpa told you once.
The water heater. That big white tank in the bathroom. It's completely full of tap water.
There's a little valve at the bottom. You open it, and water comes out. Lukewarm, a little rusty, but it comes out.
And in the toilet tank, not the bowl, there's another gallon or two of clean tap water.
You fill every pot, every bottle, every vase. Grandpa boils the water on his camping stove, just to be safe.
He pats you on the shoulder. You actually listened to him, he says. That doesn't happen often.
Around noon, you hear a helicopter. You run to the window and wave like crazy.
It flies right past. It doesn't see you. To them, you're just one of a thousand windows.
So you need something they can see from above.
With Grandpa's marker, you write huge letters on his white bedsheet. Two people. Sixteenth floor.
Then you tie it to the balcony. It flutters in the wind like a little white flag.
Your text is still spinning. Twenty-one hours now.
Eleven ten at night.
Grandpa is asleep in his armchair under three blankets. You sit next to him and listen to the city breathe. Dogs, sirens, wind.
And then you hear something else. A knocking. Faint. It's coming from the wall.
You take the flashlight out into the stairwell. The neighbors' door is warped and jammed shut.
You knock back. And from inside, a small voice calls out.
"Hello? Is someone there? My mom's not home."
It's Lina, the little girl from next door. Eight years old. Her mom was working the late shift at the hospital. She's been alone for thirty-three hours.
The door won't move an inch. But Lina's balcony is right next to yours. Only a thin divider wall between them.
You step out onto the balcony and you don't look down. A hundred and sixty feet. You don't look down.
With Grandpa's hammer, you knock a hole in the divider. Then another one. Your arm is shaking.
And then Lina climbs through, in her pajamas, with her stuffed animal under her arm. She throws her arms around your neck and won't let go.
Grandpa wakes up, sees you two and laughs. Now there are three of you. Three people, half a bathtub of water and a deck of cards.
That same night, he teaches Lina how to play rummy. She wins right away. He claims he let her win.
Tuesday. Two in the afternoon.
Since this morning, your grandpa has been different. Gray in the face. He has to sit down every few minutes.
You pick up his pill bottle. It's empty. He took the last one this morning. He didn't tell you, so you wouldn't worry.
For the first time, you're not scared for yourself. You're scared for him.
Then, in the afternoon, you hear engines. Down on the street, fire trucks pull up, and a van full of rescue dogs.
A ladder truck extends its ladder. Higher, and higher. And then it stops, way too far below you.

That's no accident. In the US, a building counts as a high-rise above seventy-five feet, because beyond that, fighting fires from outside with ladders gets really hard. That's about the seventh floor.
You're on the sixteenth. More than twice as high.
Then someone shouts through a megaphone. Every machine shuts off. The dogs sit down. The whole street goes dead silent.
A silent period. Rescuers listen with sensitive devices for signs of life. For voices. For knocking.
"Don't yell. Knock. The pipes carry the sound through the whole building."
You grab the wrench and bang it against the heating pipe. Three times. Pause. Three times. Pause.
You hold your breath. Ten seconds. Twenty.
And then, very faintly, from deep inside the building: three knocks back.
Lina jumps up and down. Grandpa closes his eyes and smiles. They know you're here.
Wednesday. Six in the morning.
But knowing isn't the same as saving. For a whole day, nothing else happens.
There's only half a bottle of water left. You give it to Lina and Grandpa. You just take one sip, to wet your lips.
After earthquakes, rescuers talk about the seventy-two hours. After that, the chance of finding trapped people alive drops with every day.
You're at hour sixty-four.
Then your phone buzzes. Nine percent battery. A message. From your mom.
I'm downstairs. I'm not leaving. Your text made it. Sometime during the night, after two and a half days.
You look down. Between all the helmets and trucks, there's a tiny figure waving with both arms.
You cry. For the first time since the quake.
In the afternoon, another aftershock hits. The strongest one since Sunday.
When the dust settles, the hole in the stairwell is bigger. It now reaches up to the fourteenth floor.
And in your living room wall, there's a crack as wide as your finger. Nobody can reach you from below anymore.
If help comes, it won't come from below. It'll come from above.
One twenty in the afternoon.
Another message. Three percent battery. Go to the roof. Helicopter in forty minutes.
The roof is eight floors up. For you, that's two minutes. For your grandpa, without his pills, it's a mountain.
Lina leads the way with the flashlight. You hold Grandpa up. Step by step. After every floor, he has to sit down.
On the twentieth floor, he tells you to go on without him.
You say no. You say the rummy game isn't over yet. And that he still owes you one.
He laughs, coughs, and gets back up. Twenty-two. Twenty-three. Twenty-four.
Then you push open the heavy steel door, and the wind hits you in the face. The roof. Nothing above you but sky.
With a piece of brick, Lina draws three giant letters on the tar. S. O. S.
Two oh two. Exactly seventy-two hours after the quake.
At first, you only hear it. That deep thumping you can feel in your stomach. Then it appears from behind the building next door.
The helicopter hovers right above you. A rescuer comes down on a cable, in a helmet and harness.
Lina goes first. She hugs her stuffed animal and waves at you as she's pulled up.
Then your grandpa. Before they strap him in, he presses something into your hand. His deck of cards.
"Take good care of these. We're not done yet."
And then you. Last. The harness pulls you up, the roof gets smaller, the city gets huge.
From up here, you can see how many buildings are damaged. And how many rooftops still have people waiting. You're one of the lucky ones.
The helicopter lands on a sports field. You jump out and run. Someone is running toward you.
Your mom holds you so tight you can barely breathe. She smells like smoke and coffee and three nights without sleep.
"I read your message a hundred times. Every time I couldn't go on."
Your grandpa goes to the hospital. New pills, an IV, two days of rest. And then he's his old self again.
Lina's mom finds her that same evening. For three days, she'd been in the ER, helping other people.
Since then, you have a drawer too. Flashlight, crank radio, a power bank, ten bottles of water. Nobody laughs at it anymore.
And every Sunday, you sit together again. You, your grandpa and Lina. With apple pie.
You never finished that rummy game. You all decided it should never really end.
